has spent the past year under intense investor scrutiny, with concerns centered on soaring capital expenditures and negative free cash flow. But according to one veteran technology analyst, the debate is shifting.
The bigger question now isn’t how much Oracle is spending—it’s how much of its AI future depends on a single customer.
Why OpenAI Matters to Oracle
Paul Meeks
, head of technology research at
Freedom Capital Markets
, believes Wall Street’s concerns have evolved as Oracle pushes deeper into AI infrastructure.

“It’s the 80-20 rule,” said Meeks. “The 80 [is] a change from a positive narrative surrounding building AI infrastructure to a negative… folks are rattling the cages about we’re not going to be able to monetize this.”
“But the 20 is you’re dealing with
OpenAI
,” he added, noting that what was once viewed as a major strategic win is now prompting questions about counterparty risk.
Meeks said Oracle’s partnership with OpenAI was initially celebrated by investors, but uncertainty surrounding OpenAI’s business trajectory has changed the conversation.

“When they announced the relationship with OpenAI a year ago, that was seen as a blessing from God,” he said. “Of course, now, some folks are saying, ‘Oh, there might be some counterparty risk there.'”
His comments come as Oracle faces growing investor scrutiny over its AI investments, balance sheet and dependence on a handful of large AI customers.

children: Oracle’s AI Risk Is Changing
Meeks argues the concern is less about Oracle’s willingness to invest than about how concentrated the payoff has become.

“Most of it is an increasing anxiety… about the inability to monetize AI infrastructure spend, particularly with Oracle… And then, this OpenAI risk, which a year ago was seen as a blessing. Now it’s saying, ‘Oh God, you have so much of your RPO tied up in OpenAI.'”
He noted that while Oracle’s more than $600 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO) is an impressive figure, “about 50% of the RPO is OpenAI.”

That concentration means Oracle’s AI narrative is becoming increasingly intertwined with the success of its largest customer. Meeks said regaining investor confidence will likely require tangible evidence that Oracle’s infrastructure investments are translating into financial returns while OpenAI continues to execute.
“They need this IPO to raise the equity, to pay bills, and the biggest bill they’ve got to pay, because it’s such a big piece of the RPO, is Oracle,” he said, referring to OpenAI.
Oracle’s AI strategy is no longer being judged solely on how much it spends building infrastructure, but on whether those investments generate durable returns across a diversified customer base.

While Meeks’ views reflect analyst opinion rather than company guidance, his comments suggest investors may increasingly watch customer concentration alongside capital spending as a key indicator of Oracle’s long-term AI execution.
